| [LIT-140](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-140.md) v2 | Large Language Models Are Stochastic Measuring Devices | Mallory (2025), DOI-10.1093/9780191998317.003.0003. The chapter argues by analogy that deep neural networks are "stochastic measuring devices". Training alters the parameters in response to data, so that the resulting configuration carries information about the data ("training is measurement"). The trained weights are a model, and generation is simulation. DNNs are stochastic because random initialisation and non-convex loss mean runs need not converge to the same weights, failing Baird's "regularity" condition. The problems of interpreting model states and generated text are therefore the familiar problems of instruments, models and simulations. The problem of interpretable AI is an instance of the coordination problem in the philosophy of measurement. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-090](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-090.md)); worth reading as the most developed instrument-centred alternative to agentive framings of LLMs, and for its tidy division into model-interpretation, text-interpretation and linking problems; it offers an analogy, not a refutation (its own words, § Interpretation and Communication), and should be read in the published OUP version where possible. |

The authors argue that distributional models answer the instability objection to meaning holism if meaning is read "differentially", as a word's relations to its nearest neighbours, and not as its position in the space. They illustrate this with two corpus-expansion demonstrations. In a ±10-word count model on Stein's The Making of Americans (about 522k tokens), adding Hemingway's "A Clean, Well-Lighted Place" (under 1,500 words) shifts every cosine value for "know" by at most about 0.0005 (e.g. 0.95231 → 0.95284 for "understand") and leaves its top-10 neighbours in the same order, while "glass" gets a new neighbourhood. True Believers ([LIT-398](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-398.md)) later withdraws exactly that relativity. Its lasting tool for this record is the "loan of intelligence" (p. 96): any theory that gives a part content owes an account of that part's reader, and "wherever a theory relies on a formulation bearing the logical marks of Intentionality, there a little man is concealed". | [LIT-446](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-446.md) | Survival and Identity | Lewis (1976), DOI-10.1525/9780520353060-002. What matters in survival is mental continuity and connectedness (the R-relation among person-stages), and it is also identity, because the two answers relate different things. Persons are maximal R-interrelated aggregates of stages, so the I-relation (being stages of one person) is the R-relation in every possible case. Fission and fusion are two persons sharing stages, counted as one by "tensed identity"; Methuselah is a continuum of overlapping 137-year persons; degrees of personal identity come from supervaluating over cut-offs for R. Against Perry: two persons, not three, took part in a fission. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-373](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-373.md)), from a scan of the 1976 printing posted on Andrew M. Bailey's "Papers by David Lewis" page, OCR'd here; worth reading as the four-dimensionalist reconciliation of Parfit with common sense, and the source of stage-sharing and counting by tensed identity. It agrees with Parfit that what matters is mental continuity and connectedness, the R-relation among person-stages, and denies that this conflicts with identity: persons are maximal R-interrelated aggregates of stages, so the relation of being stages of one person is the R-relation. Fission becomes two persons sharing their early stages, and degrees are handled by supervaluation. A reconciliation by redefinition of counting, which Lewis grants is "somewhat counterintuitive". |

It answers a manuscript of Clark's "Memento's Revenge" (the chapter before it in the same volume), restating the two marks of the cognitive and defending them against Clark's Euler-circle and "brain-tool science" objections. It adds no new argument for either mark: the fallacy is shown by one analogy (nerve and muscle), and the intracranial processing differences are asserted from consumer electronics, not measured. |
| [LIT-460](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-460.md) v2 | Role play with large language models | Shanahan, McDonell & Reynolds (2023), Nature 623:493–498. A dialogue agent is an LLM role-playing the character its prompt describes, or more exactly a simulator keeping a superposition of simulacra consistent with the conversation. Only simulacra can appear to have beliefs, goals or a self; the simulator has none, "not even simulated versions", and "it is role play all the way down". When an agent says it wants to survive there is "no-one at home". Each role-played character would carry its own theory of selfhood, which the conversation narrows; what an agent would try to preserve (hardware, process, instance) is left open. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-370](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-370.md)), in the Nature text with the arXiv v1 preprint compared; worth reading here as the source of the simulator/simulacra account that every LLM-selfhood paper in this record answers. On it nothing is a self: the simulator has no beliefs, goals or agency "of its own, not even simulated versions", and a simulacrum only role-plays a character that has them ("no-one at home"). Its one section on selfhood asks which self a role-played character would try to preserve, not what the system is, and leaves identity over time for a dialogue agent "far from clear". The denial of a self is asserted from the framing, not argued against a rival. |
| [LIT-465](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-465.md) | Simulacra as Conscious Exotica | Shanahan (2024), Inquiry 69(6):2982–3010, from arXiv:2402.12422. After Wittgenstein, consciousness words mean only what is public, so the question for an exotic entity is whether we could "engineer an encounter" with it in a shared world and what a society-wide conversation would then say. Disembodied chat agents are not even candidates; virtually embodied LLM agents could be. Tool use and memory make belief talk increasingly literal, but a chat agent has no "self worth preserving", and a role player has no "person behind the mask": its identity is a shifting distribution of roles. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-382](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-382.md)) in the arXiv v2 preprint (July 2024), not the Inquiry version of record, which returned 403; worth reading as the Wittgensteinian alternative to the evidential debate about AI consciousness. It replaces "is it conscious?" with "could we engineer an encounter with it, and how would our language adapt?", and so counts disembodied chat agents as not even candidates. On the self it is brief and pointed: a chat agent has "nothing that would qualify as a self worth preserving", lacking body, personal history and autobiographical memory, and a role-playing agent has no "person behind the mask"; its identity, "insofar as that notion even made sense", is the shifting distribution of roles. It argues by method and scenario, not evidence, and says so. |
| [LIT-466](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-466.md) | Palatable Conceptions of Disembodied Being | Shanahan (2025), arXiv:2503.16348. Asks whether consciousness talk can be stretched to disembodied, 2024-vintage LLM agents. Their time would be discrete and discontinuous, a string of unlike beads. Their "I" has two palatable referents, the model across conversations and a self confined to one conversation that "flickers into being with each user interaction", and we may slip between them. Such selves can be edited, copied and merged, and smeared across branching simulacra. Every candidate site dissolves, which Shanahan reads as Buddhist emptiness, and turns back on human selfhood. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-376](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-376.md)) in arXiv v3 (July 2025), the only text there is; worth reading as the one paper here that argues directly about what an LLM's self is, rather than whether it has one. Its answer: two conceptions are in play, a self sited in the model and "fleeting, flickering" selves sited in single conversations, and we may slip between them; every candidate site "dissolves upon close examination", and Shanahan takes that to the Buddhist conclusion that there is no inherent self, here or in us. It is avowedly "poetic", not literal, and its examples are invented usages, not data. |
| [LIT-472](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-472.md) | Understanding Institutions: The Science and Philosophy of Living Together | Guala (2016), DOI-10.1515/9781400880911. Per its publisher, a unified theory of institutions combining three views (equilibria of strategic games, regulative rules, constitutive rules), applied to money, private property and marriage. It then addresses reflexivity, realism, Verstehen and fallibilism in the social sciences, criticises Hacking's looping effects and interactive kinds, and asks whether causal and ontological dependence can demarcate social from natural science. Only the sample chapter 1 was read: it restates Hindriks & Guala's case against a rules-only account. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description, table of contents, sample chapter and index, not read: the book is not lawfully readable in full online (De Gruyter and Princeton are paywalled, and the Internet Archive has no copy). Only chapter 1, Rules, the publisher's free sample, was read; it is a lightly expanded version of the first section of Hindriks & Guala ([LIT-481](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-481.md)). It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-473](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-473.md) | Convention: A Philosophical Study | Lewis (1969), DOI-10.1002/9780470693711 (the 2002 Blackwell reissue). The founding analysis of convention as a self-perpetuating solution to a recurring coordination problem with more than one equilibrium, sustained by a system of mutual expectations rather than by agreement, with conventions of language and communication as the main application. Unread: filed from catalogue records and chapter titles; the content summary is as Hindriks & Guala and the SEP entry state it. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from catalogue records and the chapter list, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. The Harvard 1969 edition is lending-only at the Internet Archive (access-restricted, printdisabled), and the Wiley-Blackwell reissue of 2002 is paywalled. What the book argues is known here only through readings that state it (Hindriks & Guala, [LIT-481](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-481.md); the SEP entry, [LIT-487](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-487.md)), and is labelled as theirs. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-480](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-480.md) | Gender and Race: (What) Are They? (What) Do We Want Them To Be? | Haslanger (2000), Noûs 34(1):31–55. Distinguishes conceptual, descriptive and analytical answers to "what is gender/race?" and takes the analytical one: define the terms for what a feminist antiracist theory needs. S is a woman iff S is regularly observed or imagined to have bodily features presumed to indicate a female's reproductive role, this marks S in the dominant ideology for subordinate positions, and that plays a role in S's subordination; men and racialized groups are defined in parallel, ethnicity and gender in general as the non-hierarchical genus. Stipulative by design; no evidence offered. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-394](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-394.md)); worth reading as the founding statement of ameliorative ("analytical") social ontology and of gender and race as hierarchical social positions. It is short and explicit about its method: it defines woman, man and racialized group for the purposes of a feminist and antiracist theory, says so, and accepts the consequences (non-oppressed females are not women in its sense, and the goal is a world with none). Read it for the three-way distinction between conceptual, descriptive and analytical projects and for the definitional schema (marked by assumed bodily features, positioned by a dominant ideology, subordinated or privileged as a result), not for evidence: its "matters of established fact" about race are asserted without citation, and its definitions are stipulated, not discovered. |
| [LIT-481](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-481.md) | Institutions, rules, and equilibria: a unified theory | Hindriks & Guala (2015, online 2014), DOI-10.1017/S1744137414000496. Institutions are rules in equilibrium: correlated equilibria of coordination games with several equilibria, which the players represent to themselves as rules. Searle's constitutive rules ("X counts as Y in C") are obtained from a regulative rule by splitting it with a new term, a base rule (X is Y) and a status rule (if Y then Z). The new term is conservative and eliminable, so the constitutive-rules account reduces to the rules-in-equilibrium account, and Lewis's theory of theoretical terms says the term refers if the rules are true. Shown on one toy institution (first-occupancy property); general reduction asserted. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-395](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-395.md)), with the authors' reply to their six commentators in the same issue; worth reading as the shortest statement of the rules-in-equilibrium theory of institutions and of the claim that Searle's constitutive rules are regulative rules with a name added. The equilibrium half is a clear synthesis of Lewis, Aumann, Aoki and Greif. The reduction of constitutive rules is shown on one toy institution and asserted in general, and it leans on a reading of "collective acceptance" loose enough to make it hard to fail. |
| [LIT-482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-482.md) | Social ontology: Some basic principles | Searle (2006), DOI-10.1177/1463499606061731. Institutional reality is built from three primitives: collective intentionality, the assignment of function, and constitutive rules of the form "X counts as Y in C". The Y status is held only by collective acceptance, and it carries deontic powers, which are desire-independent reasons for action. Institutional facts need language because they exist only as represented. Two revisions of the 1995 book: status indicators (after De Soto), and "free-standing Y terms" (after Barry Smith), such as corporations and money without currency. In those cases there is no X, and "We accept (S has power (S does A))", a formula from later in the book, is ranked as the more general form. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-388](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-388.md)), in its parallel English printing in Papers: Revista de Sociologia 80 (2006), pp. 51–71, not in the Anthropological Theory typesetting the DOI names; worth reading as Searle's own short restatement of The Construction of Social Reality ([LIT-485](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-485.md)), and as the place where he concedes that "X counts as Y in C" is not the general form. Status functions imposed by collective acceptance carry deontic powers, and deontic powers are desire-independent reasons for action. Read it for the structure, not for an argument about collective intentionality: that is taken as a primitive and referred to his 1990 paper ([LIT-490](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-490.md)), not defended here. |
| [LIT-485](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-485.md) | The Construction of Social Reality | Searle (1995), Free Press, New York (xiii + 241 pp.). The founding book of Searle's social ontology. Per its catalogue description, it argues that some facts are independent of human observers and some require human agreement. Its chapters move from the building blocks of social reality and the creation of institutional facts through language and a general theory of institutional facts, to a defence of external realism and the correspondence theory of truth. Unread: filed from the catalogue record and contents; the record reads the theory in Searle's 2006 restatement. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from catalogue records and a library scan of the table of contents; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in print with Free Press / Simon & Schuster, the Internet Archive copies are either lending-only or unauthorised uploads, and Searle posted no draft), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. The record reads the theory through Searle's own 2006 restatement ([LIT-482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-482.md), read in full), which is the entry to start from. |
| [LIT-487](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-487.md) | Social Ontology | Epstein (2018; rev. 2024), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/social-ontology/>. A survey that splits social ontology into two inquiries: what determines (grounds) a social fact, and what constructs or "anchors" the category it falls under, likened to semantics and metasemantics. §3 surveys determination bases (psychologism, atomism, bodies and practices, physicalism, holism, flat ontologies) and reports that ontological individualism is widely assumed and recently contested. §4 surveys anchoring theories (agreement, Lewis's convention, Hart and Searle's collective acceptance, patterns, practices, language). §5 covers groups, group minds and agency, institutions, race and gender, artifacts, money, law and language. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-393](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-393.md)); worth reading as a survey: the best single map of social ontology in the record, organised around its author's distinction between what grounds a social fact (§3) and what anchors, or sets up, the category it falls under (§4). It is also the record's readable source for what The Ant Trap's grounding–anchoring framework is ([LIT-478](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-478.md) is not lawfully readable). Read it as a survey written by a partisan: Epstein's own positions organise the entry, and the critics of anchoring are named but given a sentence each. |
| [LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md) | Relational Frame Theory: Some Implications for Understanding and Treating Human Psychopathology | Barnes-Holmes, Barnes-Holmes, McHugh & Hayes (2004), International Journal of Psychology and Psychological Therapy 4(2):355–375. RFT stated briefly: humans relate events bidirectionally and arbitrarily, as a generalized operant under contextual control, so words take on the functions of what they are related to. Frames combine into networks, networks are related to networks (metaphor), rules are networks that regulate behaviour, and the self is content, process and context of verbal relations. Psychopathology is read as verbal behaviour, and ACT's acceptance, defusion and values are given RFT interpretations. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-430](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-430.md)), in place of the RFT book, [LIT-549](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-549.md); worth reading as a short statement of Relational Frame Theory by two of the book's editors, and as the paper that shows how RFT is meant to become a theory of psychopathology. Humans, unlike the animals of conditioning research, relate events bidirectionally, so a word acquires the functions of what it names. Relating is a generalized operant learned across exemplars, and its frames share mutual entailment, combinatorial entailment and the transformation of function. Rules are relational networks, and the self is three verbal relations to one's own behaviour. ACT's acceptance, defusion and values are then reinterpreted in those terms. Its clinical examples are illustrations, not data, and it says its Part 3 is "no more than a heuristic". |
| [LIT-549](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-549.md) | Relational Frame Theory: A Post-Skinnerian Account of Human Language and Cognition | Hayes, Barnes-Holmes & Roche (eds.), Kluwer Academic/Plenum, 2001. The founding book of Relational Frame Theory: human language and cognition are learned, generalized operant behaviour, the arbitrarily applicable relating of events (mutually, in combination, and with transformation of their functions) under contextual control. Eight chapters state the theory, from derived relations to rules and the self; five apply it to development, education, social processes, psychopathology and religion. Unread: registered from Crossref's chapter records, with [LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md) read in its place. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from Crossref's book and chapter records, not read; [LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md), a 21-page statement of the same theory by two of its editors, was read in its place. No lawful full text of the book was found. Springer's book page returned a "Client Challenge" bot page, Unpaywall and OpenAlex list no open copy, and Maynooth University's repository (where Barnes-Holmes and Roche deposited many RFT papers) holds no chapter of it. A copy on an Ethiopian national-library server was not used, because it is not an author, institutional or publisher deposit. The editors' own fourteen-page chapter 8, "Relational Frame Theory: A Précis" (pp. 141–154, DOI 10.1007/0-306-47638-x_8), is the part a human reader should take first; a reading of the whole book would move this to Active. |
| [LIT-625](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-625.md) | Functional Role and Truth Conditions | Block (1987), Aristotelian Society Supplementary Volume 61:157–181, the first paper of a symposium with John Campbell. Functional role semantics can explain five facts about concepts (holism of concepts and thoughts, incommensurability, limits on attributing irrationality, structure). To give Twin Earth truth conditions, a private-use theory must add a referential factor; a public-use theory must extend roles into the world with devices from the theory of reference (dominant causal source, borrowed reference, experts). Either way the result is equivalent to a two-factor theory whose internal factor is narrow meaning. Burge's arthritis cases need, in addition, functional role in a language with its structure of deference. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-492](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-492.md)); worth reading as the work the record cites as "Block 1987" ([NOTE-117](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-117.md), after Drayson): a short argument that any use theory of meaning that gets Twin Earth truth conditions right, whether it starts from private use in thought or public use in communication, ends up equivalent to a two-factor theory with a narrow, in-the-head functional role and a referential factor. It leaves room for narrow content without arguing for it, and its appendix concedes that Burge's arthritis cases need functional role in a language, structured by deference, as well as in the individual. Block says outright that he has not tried to settle whether narrow content is explanatory. |
| [LIT-630](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-630.md) | The Mind as the Software of the Brain | Block (1995), in Smith & Osherson (eds.), An Invitation to Cognitive Science, 2nd ed., vol. 3, Thinking, MIT Press, ch. 11, pp. 377–425. The computer model explains intelligence by decomposing it into ever stupider processors that bottom out in primitive processors, the only devices for which behaviourism is true. The brain is a syntactic engine driving a semantic engine, by an isomorphism between symbol transitions and rational relations among meanings, which must hold counterfactually, so a wall is not every computer. Intentionality comes from the language of thought plus functional role semantics. Stich's syntactic theory falls to the "Reductionist Cruncher", and the systems reply answers Searle, though Block doubts the Chinese system is phenomenally conscious. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-490](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-490.md)); worth reading as Block's textbook statement of what "the mind is the software of the brain" means: intelligence explained by functional decomposition into primitive processors, the brain as a syntactic engine driving a semantic engine, intentionality explained by the language of thought plus functional role semantics, and the defence of that picture against Dennett's objections, Stich's syntactic theory (by the "Reductionist Cruncher") and Searle's Chinese room. It is a survey for an introductory volume, so its arguments are compressed, but it states clearly two things the record uses: intelligence is future-oriented and intentionality past-oriented, and the computer model may give intentionality without phenomenal consciousness. |
| [LIT-648](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-648.md) | Advertisement for a Semantics for Psychology | Block (1986), Midwest Studies in Philosophy 10:615–678. A semantics for cognitive science should explain, among other things, narrow and wide meaning, what makes expressions meaningful, the relativity of meaning to representational system, learning, and how inherited meaning (of words on a page) relates to autonomous meaning (of the language of thought). Two-factor conceptual role semantics is the only approach that promises all of them: an expression's narrow meaning is its causal role in reasoning and deliberation, short-armed at the skin, and a referential factor fixes truth conditions. Conceptual role determines the nature of the referential factor but not reference. Harman's one-factor long-arm roles collapse into the same theory; Gricean and indicator semantics are either not naturalistic or fail. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-503](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-503.md)); worth reading as the main statement of two-factor conceptual role semantics: narrow meaning is an expression's conceptual role inside the head ("total causal role, abstractly described"), and a separate referential factor relates it to the world. Block argues it is the only approach that can meet eight desiderata for a semantics serving cognitive science, among them narrow content, learning, relativity to representational system, and the relation of autonomous to inherited meaning. It is an advertisement, as titled: no identity conditions for conceptual roles are given, and Block says he is "far from a true believer". |
| [LIT-774](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-774.md) | Cours de linguistique générale | Saussure (1916), Payot, compiled posthumously from students' lecture notes. The founding text of structural linguistics: the sign as an arbitrary union of signifier and signified, langue against parole, synchrony against diachrony, and value fixed by oppositions within the system, with signified and signifier each purely differential and the sign as a whole positive. Read in the third-edition text. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-594](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-594.md)), in French, from the Wikisource transcription of the third-edition text, not the 1916 first edition; worth reading as the source of the structuralist account of the sign: linguistics takes langue, the social system, as its object; the sign joins a concept and an acoustic image by an arbitrary bond, which is why it resists deliberate change and cannot resist blind change; synchrony and diachrony are irreducible; and a term's value is fixed by its oppositions to coexisting terms rather than by its signification alone (mouton against sheep and mutton). The "only differences without positive terms" holds of signified and signifier separately; the sign as a whole is called positive. The text is the editors' reconstruction from students' notes. |
| [LIT-784](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-784.md) | Translation and Relevance: Cognition and Context | Gutt (1991; 2nd ed. 2000), St. Jerome. Translation as interlingual interpretive use under Sperber and Wilson's relevance theory: a translation resembles the original in the inferences it lets an audience draw, and direct translation preserves the original's communicative clues. Not read: no lawful full text was found. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-09 from Crossref and catalogue records, not read: no lawful full text of either edition was found. HathiTrust holds the 2000 edition search-only, the Internet Archive holds no scan of either edition, and Routledge sells the reissue. Gutt's 1989 University of London thesis of the same title is listed as open access at UCL Discovery, but it is a different work and was not read as this one. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied, not on merit. No NOTE is filed. |
| [LIT-785](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-785.md) | How to Do Things with Words | Austin (1962), Clarendon Press. The William James Lectures that founded speech-act theory: some utterances do things rather than describe them, and every utterance has locutionary, illocutionary and perlocutionary aspects. Not read: no lawful full text was reachable. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-09 from catalogue records, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. The Internet Archive holds the 1962 Harvard and 1975 Clarendon editions only as controlled-lending items (access-restricted), and the unrestricted copies there are uploads by individuals of an in-copyright book, not lawful sources; the publishers offer no open access. No NOTE is filed. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-786](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-786.md) | On Linguistic Aspects of Translation | Jakobson (1959), in Brower (ed.), On Translation, Harvard University Press, pp. 232–239. The meaning of a sign is its translation into further signs; translation is intralingual, interlingual or intersemiotic. Code-units rarely have full equivalents across languages, but messages can be adequately rendered: "equivalence in difference" is the cardinal problem. All cognitive content is conveyable in any language; languages differ in what they must convey, so obligatory categories force choices that add or drop information. Poetry, where grammar and sound carry meaning, allows only creative transposition. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-614](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-614.md)): in full, from a scan of the 1959 printing posted as a course reading by the University of Toronto's Centre for Comparative Literature. Worth reading as the source of the three kinds of translation (intralingual, interlingual, intersemiotic) and of the argument that interlingual translation substitutes whole messages for messages, since code-units rarely have full equivalents. Its sharpest claim is that languages differ in what they must convey, not in what they may convey: obligatory grammatical categories force a translator to add or drop information, so a chain of translations back and forth can strip a message of its content. Limits: an essay argued from examples, with one psychological test cited second-hand; poetry is set aside as untranslatable, open only to "creative transposition". |
| [LIT-794](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-794.md) | Making It Explicit: Reasoning, Representing, and Discursive Commitment | Brandom (1994), Harvard University Press. Explains meaning by use in normative terms. Asserting is undertaking a commitment, licensing others' reassertion and taking on responsibility to show entitlement; interlocutors keep score of one another's commitments and entitlements; a claim's content is its inferential role (what it follows from, what follows from it, what it rules out). Logical vocabulary makes these implicit proprieties explicit. Skimmed: the Preface and the core of chapter 3 only. | Active — skimmed 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-622](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-622.md)); the Preface and the core of chapter 3 (pp. 141–157 and 172–193) were read, the rest of the 741 pages not. Worth reading as the source of the deontic scorekeeping model of assertion. Asserting undertakes a commitment, authorizes others to reassert it, and takes on a responsibility to show entitlement if challenged. Every interlocutor keeps a score of everyone's commitments and entitlements, so the score is doubly perspectival, and an assertion's significance is the change it makes to each score, fixed by the content's inferential role. Read it with the caveat that the reading covers the model, not the book's arguments for it (chapters 1–2, 4–9). |
| [LIT-811](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-811.md) | Assertion | Stalnaker (1978), in P. Cole (ed.), Pragmatics (Syntax and Semantics 9), Academic Press, 315–332. The source of the context set: the common ground as the set of possibilities compatible with what the participants presuppose, and an assertion's essential effect as removing the possibilities incompatible with what is said. Not read: no lawful full text was reachable. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-09 from catalogue records, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. The chapter is in Syntax and Semantics 9 (Academic Press, 1978), now digitised by Brill, whose chapter page and PDF refused access (HTTP 403); the reprint in Stalnaker's Context and Content (Oxford, 1999) is lending-only at the Internet Archive; no author or institutional copy was found. What it says is known here only through the three readings of the same day that state or quote it (Heim, [LIT-838](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-838.md), who quotes it at length; Krifka, [LIT-835](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-835.md); Veltman, [LIT-818](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-818.md)), and is labelled as theirs. No NOTE is filed. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-818](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-818.md) | Defaults in Update Semantics | Veltman (1996), J. Philos. Logic 25(3):221–261. Defines an update system (a sentence's meaning is an operation on information states), proves it reduces to static propositions exactly when it is additive, and shows epistemic "might" and "presumably" are non-persistent tests. Builds a decidable non-monotonic logic of default rules ("if φ, normally ψ") in which specificity and other priorities between conflicting defaults follow from coherence and applicability conditions on expectation frames. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-617](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-617.md)); worth reading as the programmatic statement of update semantics: the meaning of a sentence is the change it makes to an information state, and an update system is "additive", so reducible to static propositions, exactly when updates are total, idempotent, persistent, monotone and strengthening. "Might" and "presumably" fail persistence: they are tests on a state, not information about the world. Its second half is a theory of defaults in which priority between conflicting rules ("more specific wins", the Nixon diamond left open) follows from a coherence and an applicability criterion rather than being stipulated. Read the default theory as one formalisation the author himself hopes will be bettered; the framework is the lasting part. |
| [LIT-823](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-823.md) | Semantic Communication: A Survey of Its Theoretical Development | Xin, Fan & Letaief (2024), Entropy 26(2):102. A survey of semantic information theory: semantic entropy (logical probability, task-, knowledge- and context-based variants), semantic rate–distortion with meaning as a latent state behind the observation, semantic noise and semantic channel capacity, and the information bottleneck, age of information, joint source–channel coding and LLMs as tools. It records that no unified framework exists. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-619](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-619.md)); worth reading as a map of what "semantic information theory" has meant from Carnap and Bar-Hillel to deep-learning semantic communication: logical-probability and knowledge-base definitions of semantic entropy, a semantic rate–distortion function in which meaning is a hidden state S observed through X, semantic channel capacities that can exceed Shannon capacity by tolerating bit errors, and the information bottleneck, age of information, joint source–channel coding and LLMs as tools. It is a catalogue, not a synthesis: it states that no agreed framework exists, compares the definitions only informally, and does not cover rate–distortion–perception work. One formula is misstated (the bottleneck constraint is written with its inequality reversed). |
| [LIT-826](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-826.md) | Speech Acts: An Essay in the Philosophy of Language | Searle (1969), Cambridge University Press. The systematic development of Austin's speech-act theory around the hypothesis that speaking a language is engaging in rule-governed behaviour: illocutionary acts analysed by constitutive rules, with reference and predication treated as speech acts. Not read: no lawful full text was reachable. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-09 from catalogue records and the publisher's contents, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. The 1969 Cambridge edition is lending-only at the Internet Archive (access-restricted), Cambridge Core offers the book only to subscribers, and HathiTrust has no full-view copy. No NOTE is filed. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-835](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-835.md) | Performative updates and the modeling of speech acts | Krifka (2024), Synthese 203:31. Adds to Stalnaker's informative update, which filters a context set, a performative update that changes each index minimally so a proposition becomes true. Declarations are purely performative; assertions are a performative guarantee by the speaker followed by a negotiable informative update; commissives, directives, exclamatives, optatives, definitions and the locutionary act itself are modelled as index changes, and hereby marks a proposition made true by the utterance. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-602](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-602.md)); worth reading as the dynamic-semantic statement of the performative/constative distinction: an informative update removes indices from a context set (Stalnaker), a performative update changes them minimally so that a proposition holds (after Szabolcsi 1982), and so can add indices the context did not contain. A declaration is a pure performative update; an assertion is a performative update (the speaker publicly guarantees the proposition) followed by an informative update that the addressee may refuse. The same declarative sentence is structurally ambiguous between the two. Read it as a formal proposal argued from linguistic evidence (hereby, hedges, tense across languages), not as a tested theory, and note that commitment spaces, which carry the negotiation, are Krifka's other papers, not this one. |
| [LIT-838](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-838.md) | The Semantics of Definite and Indefinite Noun Phrases | Heim (1982), Ph.D. dissertation, University of Massachusetts Amherst (Garland, 1988). Indefinites and definites are variables with no quantificational force; indefinites are bound by the nearest operator, which explains donkey anaphora. Meaning is recast as file change potential on a common ground of numbered cards, and the definite/indefinite contrast becomes one felicity condition (new card versus familiar card), from which binding, existential readings, presupposition projection and narrow-scope definites follow. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-608](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-608.md)); worth reading as the founding statement of file change semantics and of the variable analysis of indefinites: an indefinite has no quantificational force of its own and is bound by whatever operator is nearest (an adverb of quantification, a determiner, the unpronounced necessity operator of a bare conditional), which is what makes donkey sentences come out right. Its third chapter replaces truth conditions by file change potentials, operations on a structured common ground of numbered cards, and derives the definite/indefinite contrast from one felicity condition: an indefinite opens a new card, a definite must update a familiar one. Read it as an argued theory with worked examples and stated open problems (specific indefinites, weak crossover, accommodation), not as a closed system. |
| [LIT-841](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-841.md) | Semantic Unification: A Sheaf Theoretic Approach to Natural Language | Abramsky & Sadrzadeh (2014), [ARXIV-1403.3351](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.3351), in the Lambek Festschrift (LNCS 8222, pp. 1–13). Models basic Discourse Representation Structures as sections of a presheaf of consistent literals over (vocabulary, variables), an anaphoric resolution as a cover by variable maps, and the meaning of a discourse as the gluing of its sentences' sections, unique when it exists. Failure to glue is inconsistency, not contextuality in the Abramsky–Brandenburger sense; competing resolutions are competing covers, ranked in the probabilistic section by corpus counts. | Active — read in full 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-644](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-644.md)); worth reading as the first paper to model discourse meaning as sheaf-theoretic gluing, and as the record's earliest bridge between the Abramsky–Brandenburger framework and natural-language semantics. A basic Discourse Representation Structure is a section of a presheaf of consistent literals; a choice of anaphoric resolution is a cover, a jointly surjective family of variable maps; and the meaning of the discourse is the gluing, which is unique when it exists (Proposition 1, its only result). Its "contextuality" is context dependence, not the failure of a compatible family to glue: the only obstruction it exhibits is inconsistency of literals. Its probabilistic section ranks candidate covers by summed corpus counts rather than gluing distributions. Short and preliminary by its own account. |
